docs.title: Loom 🧵
docs.text:
loom is a high-performance, graph-based AI workflow engine for Go. It allows you to build complex agentic systems by defining multi-step workflows as directed graphs, seamlessly connecting them to any large language model, and persisting execution state for long-running or interrupted tasks.

Unlike linear chains, loom provides a robust, state-first architecture inspired by state machines, making it easy to build agents that can loop, branch, and resume exactly where they left off.

docs.title: Key Features
docs.text:
• 🕸️ Graph-based Workflows: Define agents as directed graphs with nodes, conditional branching, and route edges.
  • 🔀 Parallel Execution (Fan-out / Fan-in): Concurrently run multiple downstream branches with isolated state copies and deterministic command resolution.
  • 🧩 Composable Sub-graphs: Nest graphs as first-class nodes using AsNode and state adapters with MapNode, complete with hierarchical LangGraph-style checkpoint namespaces.
  • 🛡️ Execution Safety & Middleware: Guard against runaway cycles with WithMaxSteps / ErrMaxStepsExceeded and inject resilience with RetryMiddleware and custom node middleware.
  • 💾 State Persistence: Built-in checkpointing with support for PostgreSQL and SQLite.
  • 📺 Real-time Streaming: First-class support for token-level streaming and event-based updates.
  • 🧠 Advanced Memory Management: Intelligently condense long conversations and trim message history.
  • ⚖️ Decision & Embedding Models: First-class System One probabilistic decision models (decision) and multimodal vector embeddings (embedding).
  • 📚 RAG & Semantic Memory: Built-in document loaders and splitters (document), vector stores (vectorstore), composable retrievers (retriever), and semantic KV stores (store).
  • 🔌 Provider Agnostic: One interface for OpenAI, Anthropic, Ollama, Google Gemini, and TypeSafe AI.
  • 🔌 MCP Support: Native integration with the Model Context Protocol for tools, resources, and prompts.
  • 🛠️ Tool Integration: Native support for tool calling and tool-use loops.
  • 🛡️ Type Safe: Built from the ground up with Go generics for maximum developer productivity.

docs.title: Documentation Overview
docs.text: Guide Description 🚀 Quick Start Build your first directed agent graph in minutes. 🕸️ Graph Workflows Deep dive into graph state, commands, parallel fan-out/fan-in, sub-graphs (AsNode/MapNode), execution safety (WithMaxSteps), and middleware (RetryMiddleware). 💬 Conversations Manage multimodal messages and conversation history. 🧠 LLM Package Work with the provider-agnostic Model API and Registry. ⚖️ Decision Models Fast System One probabilistic classifiers and routers. 🧭 Embedding Models Dense text and multimodal embeddings. 💾 Persistent Store Namespaced key-value storage with semantic vector search. 📚 RAG Pipelines Document loaders, splitters, vector stores, and rankers. 💾 Persistence & State Durable checkpoints with SQLite and PostgreSQL. 🤝 Human-in-the-Loop Interrupt patterns, state updates, and review workflows. 🛠️ Tools & Streaming Register tools and consume token-level event streams. 🔍 Observability Visualize workflows and inspect execution metrics in Loom Studio.

docs.title: Why Loom?
docs.text:
Loom is designed for developers who need more control than what simple chains or "black-box" agent frameworks offer. By treating your AI workflow as a state machine, Loom gives you:

  1. Explicit Control: You define exactly how the state transitions between nodes.
  2. Durability: Every step is checkpointed, so your agents can survive crashes or wait for human input.
  3. Observability: Built-in tools to visualize your graphs and trace every token and tool call.

Get Started with the Quick Start Guide →

docs.title: Installation 📦
docs.text: Loom is a Go library. To include it in your project, use go get.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Go: 1.23 or higher is recommended (Loom uses generics and modern Go features).
  • Environment: Linux, macOS, or Windows.

docs.title: Basic Installation
docs.text: go get github.com/masterkeysrd/loom

docs.title: LLM Providers
docs.text:
Depending on which LLM providers you intend to use, you may need to set specific environment variables for authentication.

Provider Requirement OpenAI OPENAI_API_KEY Anthropic ANTHROPIC_API_KEY Google Gemini GOOGLE_API_KEY Ollama Local Ollama instance running

docs.title: Persistence Backends
docs.text: Loom supports SQLite and PostgreSQL for checkpointing. These are optional but required if you want state persistence.

docs.title: SQLite
docs.text:
Requires the github.com/mattn/go-sqlite3 driver.

go get github.com/mattn/go-sqlite3

docs.title: PostgreSQL
docs.text: Requires a standard PostgreSQL connection string.

docs.title: Development Setup
docs.text:
If you plan to contribute to Loom or run the documentation locally, you can use the provided Makefile to simplify the setup.

# Install all development dependencies (Go modules and MkDocs)
make install

# Start the documentation server
make docs-serve

Available commands: - make generate: Run code generation for LLM profiles. - make test: Run all tests with race detection. - make clean: Cleanup logs and temporary files.

Once installed , proceed to the Quick Start Guide to build your first agent!

docs.title: Conversations & Messages 💬
docs.text: In Loom, a conversation is represented as an ordered list of messages. Because Loom is "state-first," these messages are typically stored in your GraphState and passed to LLMs to provide context.

docs.title: 1. Message Roles
docs.text:
Loom defines four core roles, each representing a different participant in the conversation:

Role Description Concrete Type System High-level instructions for the model (e.g., "You are a helpful assistant"). message.System User Messages sent by the human user. message.User Assistant Responses generated by the AI model. message.Assistant Tool The result of an external tool execution. message.Tool

docs.title: Creating Messages
docs.text:
import "github.com/masterkeysrd/loom/message"

systemMsg := message.NewSystemText("You are a math tutor.")
userMsg   := message.NewUserText("What is the square root of 144?")

docs.title: 2. Content Blocks
docs.text: Loom messages are composed of one or more Blocks. This flexible structure supports multimodal inputs and advanced features like "chain-of-thought" thinking.

docs.title: Text Blocks
docs.text:
The most common block type, used for simple text.

block := &message.TextBlock{Text: "Hello!"}

docs.title: Multimodal Blocks (Images, Documents)
docs.text:
You can attach images, PDFs, or other media to a user message.

imageMsg := message.NewUserImage(imageData, "image/png")
// OR via URL
imageMsg := message.NewUserImageURL("https://example.com/photo.jpg")

docs.title: Thinking Blocks
docs.text:
Some models (like Claude 3.5 or Gemini 2.0) can return their internal reasoning. Loom surfaces this as a ThinkingBlock.

// Access the thinking part of an assistant response
thinking := assistantMsg.Content.Thought()

docs.title: 3. Managing History (MessageList)
docs.text:
A MessageList is a specialized slice of messages that provides critical functionality for state management and persistence. Always use MessageList instead of a raw []message.Message when storing history in your Graph State.

type MyState struct {
    History message.MessageList `json:"history"`
}

docs.title: Why use MessageList?
docs.text:
1. Polymorphic Serialization: MessageList automatically handles the complex task of serializing different message types (User, Assistant, etc.) into a single JSON array with a "role" discriminator.
  2. Type-Safe Deserialization: When loading a checkpoint from a database (SQL or PG), MessageList ensures that raw JSON is correctly restored into the proper Go structs.
  3. Fluent Helpers: Provides methods like Last() and Text() to easily access content without range loops.
history := message.MessageList{
    message.NewSystemText("..."),
    message.NewUserText("..."),
}

// Add a new response
history = append(history, assistantResponse)

docs.title: 4. Token Metrics
docs.text:
Loom tracks token usage for every assistant response. This information is attached to the message.Assistant struct.

if resp.Metrics != nil {
    fmt.Printf("Input: %d, Output: %d, Total: %d, Estimated Cost: %s\n",
        resp.Metrics.Tokens.Input,
        resp.Metrics.Tokens.Output,
        resp.Metrics.TotalTokens,
        resp.Metrics.TotalCost)
}

docs.title: 5. Message Extensions & Metadata
docs.text: Loom provides two ways to attach auxiliary information to a message:

docs.title: Extensions (Type-Safe Hints)
docs.text:
Extensions are provider-specific structs that influence model behavior. Unlike raw metadata, Extensions are type-safe and are automatically restored to their concrete types when loaded from storage.

Loom provides two methods for adding extensions:

  1. WithExtension (Fluent): Available on concrete message types (User, Assistant, etc.). It returns the same concrete type, allowing for method chaining without type erasure.
  2. AddExtension (Polymorphic): Available on the Message interface. Use this when you are working with a generic message object.
// 1. Fluent usage (preserves *message.User type)
msg := message.NewUserText("Analyze this...").
    WithExtension(&loomanthropic.MessageCache{Enabled: true})

// 2. Interface usage
var m message.Message = msg
m.AddExtension(&someother.Extension{})

docs.title: Metadata (Arbitrary Data)
docs.text:
Metadata is a simple map[string]any for application-level data (IDs, timestamps, custom flags) that doesn't need a formal schema.

msg.Metadata["session_id"] = "xyz-123"

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• Roles: Use System, User, Assistant, and Tool to distinguish participants.
  • Blocks: Mix and match TextBlock, ImageBlock, and ThinkingBlock for rich interactions.
  • MessageList: Use this type to manage and persist your conversation history in your graph state.

docs.title: Custom Providers (Advanced) 🛠️
docs.text: Loom is designed to be provider-agnostic. While it comes with built-in support for OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini, and Ollama, you can easily add support for any other LLM backend by implementing the llm.Provider interface.

docs.title: 1. The Provider Interface
docs.text:
To create a custom provider, you must implement the following interface:

type Provider interface {
    profile.Provider

    Name() string
    Stream(context.Context, *Request) (StreamResponse, error)
}

docs.title: Optional: Cache Management
docs.text:
If your provider supports explicit resource management for context caching, you can optionally implement the CacheManager interface:

type CacheManager interface {
    CreateCache(context.Context, *Request) (string, error)
    DeleteCache(context.Context, string) error
}

docs.title: Optional: Extensions
docs.text:
If your provider has specialized features, you should define your own extension structs.

  1. Define the struct: It must implement either llm.Extension or message.Extension.
  2. Implement ExtensionID(): Return a unique string (e.g. myprovider.feature).
  3. Register (Message level only): If it's a message-level extension, call message.RegisterExtension in your init() function so it can be restored from JSON.
func init() {
    message.RegisterExtension(func() message.Extension { return &MyMsgExt{} })
}

docs.title: 2. Implementing the Stream Method
docs.text:
The core of a provider is the Stream method. It takes a generic llm.Request and returns an iterator over message.AssistantChunk values.

func (p *MyCustomProvider) Stream(ctx context.Context, req *llm.Request) (llm.StreamResponse, error) {
    // 1. Translate llm.Request to your provider's specific API format
    apiReq := translate(req)

    // 2. Call your backend's streaming API
    resp, _ := p.client.CallStreaming(ctx, apiReq)

    // 3. Return an iterator
    return func(yield func(message.AssistantChunk, error) bool) {
        for {
            chunk, err := resp.Next()
            if err != nil {
                yield(message.AssistantChunk{}, err)
                return
            }

            // 4. Translate back to Loom's AssistantChunk
            loomChunk := translateBack(chunk)
            if !yield(loomChunk, nil) {
                return
            }
        }
    }, nil
}

docs.title: 3. Mapping Messages & Tools
docs.text: Most of the work in creating a provider involves mapping between Loom's block-based message system and the provider's specific message format (e.g., Anthropic's ContentBlock vs OpenAI's ToolCall).

docs.title: Key Mapping Areas:
docs.text:
• Multimodal Content: Mapping message.ImageBlock to the provider's base64 or URL format.
  • Tool Definitions: Translating tool.Definition into the provider's JSON schema format.
  • Tool Calls: Capturing tool call IDs and arguments from the stream.

docs.title: 4. Registering Your Provider
docs.text:
Once implemented, you can register your provider with the llm.Registry to make it available to the rest of your application.

registry := llm.NewRegistry()
registry.Register("my-provider", func() (llm.Provider, error) {
    return &MyCustomProvider{}, nil
})

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• Implementing a custom provider allows Loom to talk to any internal or specialized LLM API.
  • Focus on accurate mapping of llm.Request and message.AssistantChunk.
  • Use the providers/openai or providers/anthropic packages as reference implementations.

docs.title: Decision Models ⚖️
docs.text:
The decision package introduces a first-class System One / Decision Model abstraction for Loom.

While Large Language Models excels at open-ended generative tasks, multi-turn reasoning, and conversational chat ("System Two"), modern AI workflows frequently require fast, deterministic, probabilistic decisions ("System One")—such as intent routing, guardrails, policy enforcement, classification, and triage.

Decision models evaluate structured questions against an input context (arbitrary Go state structs, plain text strings, or multimodal images) and return calibrated probabilities, confidence scores, and categorical selections without the latency, token overhead, and parsing fragility of open-ended generation.

docs.title: System One vs. System Two
docs.text: Dimension System One (decision) System Two (llm) Primary Task Fast classification, predicates, scoring, routing Generative responses, reasoning traces, tool loops Output Type Calibrated probabilities, choices, ordinal scores Open-ended text, streaming tokens, tool calls Latency Extremely low (< 100ms on native backends) Higher (seconds, token streaming) Deterministic Structure Strongly typed Answer structs Freeform text or schema validation Uncertainty Calibration Explicit probabilities & Shannon entropy confidence Logprobs or heuristic estimation

docs.title: 1. Core Abstractions
docs.text:
• Provider: The backend implementation that executes decision evaluations. Native backends include OpenAI Decisions, Ollama SystemOne, and TypeSafe AI; any LLM can also be adapted.
  • Model: The high-level wrapper configured with a provider and model name. Supports single-question shortcuts, batch evaluations, and middleware chains.
  • Question: The question definition:
  • Predicate: Binary true/false question with probability and criteria descriptions.
  • Choice: Categorical classification selecting among discrete options with probability distributions.
  • Score: Ordinal rating evaluated across an ordered list of descriptive levels.
  • Answer: The calibrated result containing probabilities, selected choices, expected score, entropy-based confidence, and refusal status.
  • PredicateEdge / ChoiceRouteEdge: Graph edges that integrate decision evaluations directly into Loom workflow graphs.

docs.title: OpenAI Native Decisions API
docs.text:
OpenAI exposes dedicated decision endpoints (/v1/decisions) optimized for low-latency probabilistic evaluations using models such as gpt-6-luna.

Loom's loomopenai.Provider implements decision.Provider out of the box:

import (
    "github.com/masterkeysrd/loom/decision"
    "github.com/masterkeysrd/loom/providers/openai"
)

// Uses OPENAI_API_KEY from environment
provider, err := loomopenai.NewDefaultProvider()
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}

// Pass provider directly to decision.NewModel
model, err := decision.NewModel(provider, "gpt-6-luna", nil)

docs.title: Ollama Native SystemOne API
docs.text:
Ollama provides local, private inference via the native /v1/systemone API using lightweight models such as nimble, clef, and clef-flash.

Loom's loomollama.Provider implements decision.Provider out of the box:

import (
    "github.com/masterkeysrd/loom/decision"
    "github.com/masterkeysrd/loom/providers/ollama"
)

// Connects to http://localhost:11434 by default
provider, err := loomollama.NewDefaultProvider()
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}

// Pass provider directly to decision.NewModel
model, err := decision.NewModel(provider, "nimble", nil)

docs.title: TypeSafe AI Native SystemOne API
docs.text:
TypeSafe AI provides dedicated, high-speed System One endpoints (POST https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone and GET https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/models) specifically architected for deterministic probabilistic decision-making.

Loom's loomtypesafe.Provider implements decision.Provider and profile.Provider out of the box:

import (
    "github.com/masterkeysrd/loom/decision"
    loomtypesafe "github.com/masterkeysrd/loom/providers/typesafe"
)

// Uses TYPESAFE_API_KEY from environment
provider, err := loomtypesafe.NewDefaultProvider()
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}

// Pass provider directly to decision.NewModel with jev-latest
model, err := decision.NewModel(provider, loomtypesafe.ModelJevLatest, nil)

Features: - Ultra-low cost: $0.042 per 1M input tokens ($0 output tokens). - Purpose-built models: loomtypesafe.ModelJevLatest ("jev-latest"), loomtypesafe.ModelJevPreview ("jev-preview"), loomtypesafe.ModelJev1_14_0 ("jev-1.14.0"), and loomtypesafe.ModelJev1_13_0 ("jev-1.13.0"). - Extended context extension: Use loomtypesafe.LongContext{Enabled: true} to raise context limits from 64k to 262k tokens. - Payload optimization & retries: Automatic gzip compression for requests $\ge$ 1 KiB, exponential retries on 429 and 529. - Modality: Text and structured JSON state (multimodal images not supported).

docs.title: LLM Fallback Adapter
docs.text:
If your preferred provider does not offer a native decision endpoint (e.g., Anthropic Claude or Google Gemini), you can adapt any standard llm.Model into a decision model using decision.NewFromLLM.

The adapter leverages constrained structured outputs (WithStructuredOutput) and automatically computes calibrated confidence scores using normalized Shannon entropy:

import (
    "github.com/masterkeysrd/loom/decision"
    "github.com/masterkeysrd/loom/llm"
    "github.com/masterkeysrd/loom/providers/anthropic"
)

anthropicProvider, _ := loomanthropic.NewDefaultProvider()
llmModel := llm.NewModel(anthropicProvider, "claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022")

// Wrap LLM model with the adapter
model, err := decision.NewFromLLM(llmModel, nil)

docs.title: 3. Single-Question Shortcuts
docs.text: For common decision patterns, Model exposes dedicated single-question helper methods:

docs.title: Binary Predicate (Check)
docs.text:
Evaluates whether a statement or condition is true:

ctx := context.Background()
input := decision.Text("Customer: 'I would like to cancel my subscription and get a refund.'")

ans, err := model.Check(ctx, input, "Is the customer requesting subscription cancellation?")
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}

if ans.Passed(0.80) {
    fmt.Printf("Cancellation confirmed (probability: %.2f, confidence: %.2f)\n", ans.Probability, ans.Confidence)
}

docs.title: Categorical Choice (Choose)
docs.text:
Selects the best matching category from a list of options:

choices := []decision.Option{
    decision.Opt("billing", "Billing queries, invoices, payment methods, or refunds"),
    decision.Opt("technical", "Software errors, bug reports, system outages"),
    decision.Opt("general", "General product inquiries and feature questions"),
}

ans, err := model.Choose(ctx, input, "Classify customer support ticket", choices)
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}

fmt.Printf("Selected category: %s (confidence: %.2f)\n", ans.Choice, ans.Confidence)
fmt.Printf("Probability for 'billing': %.2f\n", ans.Prob("billing"))

docs.title: Ordinal Rating (Rate)
docs.text:
Evaluates an item across an ordered scale of descriptive levels, returning both level probabilities and a probability-weighted expected score:

levels := []decision.Level{
    decision.Lvl("low", "Low urgency; standard inquiry or casual question"),
    decision.Lvl("medium", "Moderate urgency; account issue or unexpected behavior"),
    decision.Lvl("high", "High urgency; critical service failure or active security issue"),
}

ans, err := model.Rate(ctx, input, "Assess ticket urgency level", levels)
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}

top, _ := ans.TopLevel()
fmt.Printf("Expected Score: %.2f / %d\n", ans.Score, len(levels)-1)
fmt.Printf("Normalized Score [0..1]: %.2f\n", ans.NormalizedScore())
fmt.Printf("Top Level: %s (p=%.2f)\n", top.Label, top.Probability)

docs.title: 4. Batch Evaluation
docs.text:
When you need multiple answers evaluated against the same input context, Evaluate runs them in a single network roundtrip:

type OrderDetails struct {
    OrderID      string  `json:"order_id"`
    Amount       float64 `json:"amount"`
    ShippingCity string  `json:"shipping_city"`
    IsNewAccount bool    `json:"is_new_account"`
}

input := decision.State(OrderDetails{
    OrderID:      "ORD-7749",
    Amount:       4850.00,
    ShippingCity: "International Freight Forwarder",
    IsNewAccount: true,
})

resp, err := model.Evaluate(ctx, input,
    decision.Predicate("high_fraud_risk", "Evaluate whether this order exhibits high risk of credit fraud").
        WithCriteria("New account with large order to freight forwarder", "Verified user with consistent history"),
    decision.Choice("review_action", "Determine required risk mitigation action",
        decision.Opt("auto_approve", "Safe to process immediately"),
        decision.Opt("manual_review", "Hold for fraud analyst inspection"),
        decision.Opt("decline", "High certainty fraud; reject transaction"),
    ),
    decision.Score("risk_score", "Rate fraud risk on a 4-point scale",
        decision.Lvl("safe", "Normal legitimate pattern"),
        decision.Lvl("guarded", "Minor irregularities present"),
        decision.Lvl("elevated", "Multiple suspicious indicators"),
        decision.Lvl("critical", "Severe fraud indicators"),
    ),
)
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}

if fraudAns, ok := resp.Answer("high_fraud_risk"); ok {
    fmt.Printf("Fraud Flag: %v (p=%.2f)\n", fraudAns.Passed(0.70), fraudAns.Probability)
}
if actionAns, ok := resp.Answer("review_action"); ok {
    fmt.Printf("Recommended Action: %s (confidence: %.2f)\n", actionAns.Choice, actionAns.Confidence)
}
if scoreAns, ok := resp.Answer("risk_score"); ok {
    fmt.Printf("Risk Score: %.2f (normalized: %.2f)\n", scoreAns.Score, scoreAns.NormalizedScore())
}

docs.title: 5. Multimodal Image Evaluation
docs.text:
Decision inputs support images via WithImages, allowing decision models to inspect visual evidence alongside text prompts or structured state:

licenseImage, _ := os.ReadFile("driver_license.jpg")

input := decision.Text("Verify driver's license upload for KYC identity verification").
    WithImages(
        message.ImageData("image/jpeg", licenseImage),
    )

ans, err := model.Check(ctx, input, "Is the ID document clearly legible and unexpired?")
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}

if ans.Passed(0.90) {
    fmt.Println("KYC document verified.")
} else {
    fmt.Println("Document rejected or requires manual inspection.")
}

docs.title: 6. Interpreting Calibrated Answers
docs.text: The Answer struct provides helper methods to interpret probabilistic results:

docs.title: Probability & Passing Thresholds
docs.text:
For binary predicates, Passed(threshold) verifies that the question was not refused and its probability satisfies your threshold:

if ans.Passed(0.85) {
    // Proceed with high confidence
}

docs.title: Choice Probabilities
docs.text:
Retrieve specific choice probabilities via Prob(value):

pAdmin := ans.Prob("admin")
pUser := ans.Prob("user")

docs.title: Ordinal Scores
docs.text:
• ans.Score: Probability-weighted expected score ($\sum i \cdot P(i)$).
  • ans.NormalizedScore(): Expected score scaled to $[0.0, 1.0]$.
  • ans.TopLevel(): Returns the LevelProbability with the highest probability.

docs.title: Confidence & Refusals
docs.text:
• ans.Confidence: Normalized Shannon entropy concentration ($1 - H(p)/\ln(N)$) clamped between 0.0 (maximum uncertainty) and 1.0 (complete certainty).
  • ans.Refused: Indicates the model refused to evaluate the question (due to safety filters, unanswerable queries, or missing context).

docs.title: 7. Workflow Graph Routing Integration
docs.text: Decision models integrate directly with Loom workflow graphs (graph.Builder) via PredicateEdge and ChoiceRouteEdge.

docs.title: Conditional Binary Branching (PredicateEdge)
docs.text:
Use decision.AddConditionalEdge to route workflow execution based on a binary decision:

type OrderState struct {
    Amount    float64 `json:"amount"`
    UserEmail string  `json:"user_email"`
    Action    string  `json:"action"`
}

func (s OrderState) Copy() OrderState { return s }

builder := graph.New[OrderState]()

builder.AddNode("validate", validateOrderNode)
builder.AddNode("require_2fa", prompt2FANode)
builder.AddNode("process_payment", chargeCardNode)

// Route from "validate": if high risk, go to "require_2fa", otherwise "process_payment"
edge := decision.NewConditionalEdge(
    decisionModel,
    "require_2fa", // Next node when predicate passes threshold
    "Is this transaction unusually high-value or suspect?",
    0.75,          // Confidence threshold
    func(s OrderState) decision.Input {
        return decision.State(s)
    },
).WithElse("process_payment") // Fallback node when below threshold or refused

decision.AddConditionalEdge(builder, "validate", edge)

docs.title: Categorical Route Edge (ChoiceRouteEdge)
docs.text:
Use decision.AddRouteEdge to branch execution across multiple nodes with confidence safeguards and a designated fallback route:

routeEdge := decision.NewRouteEdge(
    decisionModel,
    "Determine the department responsible for handling this inquiry",
    []decision.Option{
        decision.Opt("billing", "Payment, billing questions, invoices"),
        decision.Opt("tech", "Software defects, outages, API errors"),
        decision.Opt("sales", "Pricing, sales inquiries, new features"),
    },
    map[string]string{
        "billing": "billing_agent",
        "tech":    "technical_support_agent",
        "sales":   "sales_agent",
    },
    func(s OrderState) decision.Input {
        return decision.Text(s.UserEmail)
    },
).
    WithMinConfidence(0.70).          // Require at least 70% confidence
    WithFallback("human_triage_queue") // Route here on low confidence, refusal, or unmapped choice

decision.AddRouteEdge(builder, "classify_inquiry", routeEdge)

docs.title: 8. Observability & Telemetry
docs.text:
Decision models include built-in OpenTelemetry instrumentation via TelemetryMiddleware:

  • Client Spans: Every decision request records a span named decision {model} with semantic conventions:
  • gen_ai.operation.name = "decision"
  • gen_ai.provider.name = "<provider>"
  • gen_ai.request.model = "<model>"
  • decision.question_count = <int>
  • Token Metrics: Input and output token usage, cache reads, and estimated costs are automatically reported to OpenTelemetry metrics.
  • Streaming Events: When a stream.Writer is attached to the context, on_decision events are published with the evaluation response and metadata source decision:<model>.

docs.title: Embedding Models 🧭
docs.text:
The embedding package provides a unified abstraction for generating dense vector representations (embedding.Vector) from text and multimodal content across cloud and local providers.

Embedding models map inputs—such as sentences, document chunks, images, or audio—into a shared vector space where semantically related items sit close together. These vectors power semantic search, Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), classification, clustering, and long-term agent memory.

docs.title: 1. Core Abstractions
docs.text:
• Provider: The backend implementation that executes embedding requests (loomopenai, loomgenai, loomollama).
  • Model: The high-level wrapper around a Provider and model name. Provides single-query and batch-document helpers, dimension and task configuration, automatic token cost calculation, and middleware chains.
  • Vector: A []float32 slice with built-in vector math methods (CosineSimilarity, Dot, EuclideanDistance, Normalize, Float64, Dimension).
  • Input: A single item to embed. Supports plain text (embedding.Text, embedding.Texts) as well as multimodal message.Block parts (embedding.Image, embedding.ImageURL, embedding.Multimodal, Input.WithParts).
  • TaskType: Optional hint informing task-aware models how vectors will be used (TaskRetrievalQuery, TaskRetrievalDocument, TaskSemanticSimilarity, TaskClassification, TaskClustering).

docs.title: OpenAI Embeddings API
docs.text:
OpenAI provides hosted text embedding models (text-embedding-3-small, text-embedding-3-large, text-embedding-ada-002) with Matryoshka dimension reduction support.

import (
    "github.com/masterkeysrd/loom/embedding"
    loomopenai "github.com/masterkeysrd/loom/providers/openai"
)

// Uses OPENAI_API_KEY from environment
provider, err := loomopenai.NewDefaultProvider()
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}

model, err := embedding.NewModel(provider, "text-embedding-3-small", nil)

docs.title: Google Gemini Embeddings API
docs.text:
Google Gemini (gemini-embedding-001, gemini-embedding-2) supports task-aware embeddings (TaskType), configurable output dimensionality, and multimodal inputs (text, images, audio, video, and PDF documents).

import (
    "context"
    "github.com/masterkeysrd/loom/embedding"
    loomgenai "github.com/masterkeysrd/loom/providers/genai"
)

// Uses GOOGLE_API_KEY from environment
provider, err := loomgenai.NewDefaultProvider(context.Background())
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}

model, err := embedding.NewModel(provider, "gemini-embedding-001", nil)

docs.title: Ollama Local Embeddings API
docs.text:
Ollama runs open-weights embedding models locally (nomic-embed-text, mxbai-embed-large, bge-m3, all-minilm, qwen3-embedding) via /api/embed.

import (
    "github.com/masterkeysrd/loom/embedding"
    loomollama "github.com/masterkeysrd/loom/providers/ollama"
)

// Connects to http://127.0.0.1:11434 by default
provider, err := loomollama.NewDefaultProvider()
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}

model, err := embedding.NewModel(provider, "nomic-embed-text", nil)

docs.title: 3. Embedding Queries and Documents
docs.text:
In retrieval workflows, indexing documents and embedding search queries are the two primary operations. Model provides dedicated helpers that automatically apply TaskRetrievalDocument and TaskRetrievalQuery:

ctx := context.Background()

// 1. Batch-embed documents
docs := []string{
    "Loom orchestrates stateful AI workflows using directed graphs.",
    "Checkpointers persist graph execution state to SQLite or PostgreSQL.",
    "Decision models evaluate fast System One predicates and choices.",
}
docVectors, err := model.EmbedDocuments(ctx, docs)
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}

// 2. Embed a single search query
queryVector, err := model.EmbedQuery(ctx, "How is workflow state persisted?")
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}

// 3. Score similarity using Vector methods
for i, docVec := range docVectors {
    score := queryVector.CosineSimilarity(docVec)
    fmt.Printf("[%.4f] %s\n", score, docs[i])
}

If you also need token usage and cost metrics, call model.Embed directly to receive the full *embedding.Response:

resp, err := model.Embed(ctx, embedding.Texts("first chunk", "second chunk"))
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}

fmt.Printf("Generated %d vectors (tokens: %d, cost: %s)\n",
    len(resp.Embeddings),
    resp.Metrics.Tokens.Input,
    resp.Metrics.TotalCost,
)

docs.title: 4. Configuring Dimensions & Task Types
docs.text:
Many modern embedding models support truncating vectors to a smaller dimensionality (Dimensions) to reduce vector storage size and speed up similarity comparisons:

// Configure defaults on a cloned model
model512 := model.
    WithDimensions(512).
    WithTaskType(embedding.TaskSemanticSimilarity)

// Or pass per-call options
vec, err := model.EmbedQuery(
    ctx,
    "semantic search query",
    embedding.WithDimensionsOption(256),
    embedding.WithTaskTypeOption(embedding.TaskRetrievalQuery),
)

docs.title: 5. Multimodal Embeddings
docs.text:
Models such as Google's gemini-embedding-2 can embed images, audio, video, and documents directly into the same vector space as text:

import (
    "github.com/masterkeysrd/loom/embedding"
    "github.com/masterkeysrd/loom/message"
)

// Embed a single inline image
imgVec, err := model.EmbedInput(ctx, embedding.Image(imageBytes, "image/png"))

// Embed text combined with multiple media blocks
combined := embedding.Text("Architecture diagram and voice note").WithParts(
    &message.ImageBlock{Data: imageBytes, MIMEType: "image/png"},
    &message.AudioBlock{Data: audioBytes, MIMEType: "audio/mp3"},
)
vec, err := model.EmbedInput(ctx, combined)

docs.title: 6. Vector Similarity & Math Operations
docs.text:
embedding.Vector ([]float32) includes built-in methods for comparing and transforming vectors without external dependencies:

Method Description v.Dimension() int Returns the number of elements in the vector (len(v)). v.CosineSimilarity(other Vector) float32 Computes cosine similarity $\frac{v \cdot \text{other}}{|v| |\text{other}|}$. Returns 0 on dimension mismatch or zero norm. v.Dot(other Vector) float32 Computes the inner dot product $\sum v_i \cdot \text{other}_i$. v.EuclideanDistance(other Vector) float32 Computes the $L_2$ distance $\sqrt{\sum (v_i - \text{other}_i)^2}$. v.Normalize() Vector Returns a new $L_2$-normalized unit vector (\|v\| = 1). v.Float64() []float64 Converts the []float32 vector into a []float64 slice.

docs.title: 7. Middleware & Observability
docs.text:
Like llm.Model and decision.Model, embedding.Model attaches TelemetryMiddleware by default and supports custom embedding.Middleware chains:

customModel := model.WithMiddleware(func(next embedding.Embedder) embedding.Embedder {
    return func(ctx context.Context, req *embedding.Request) (*embedding.Response, error) {
        log.Printf("embedding %d inputs with model %s", len(req.Inputs), req.Model)
        return next(ctx, req)
    }
})
  • OpenTelemetry Spans & Metrics: Automatically records embed {model} client spans (gen_ai.operation.name = "embeddings") and GenAI duration/token usage histograms.
  • Stream Writer Integration: Emits on_embedding events when a stream.Writer is attached to ctx.

docs.title: Graph Workflows 🕸️
docs.text:
The graph package is the core execution engine of Loom. It provides primitives for defining, executing, streaming, and persisting multi-step AI agent workflows as directed graphs.

Loom is built on a State-First architecture. Rather than managing sprawling control flow, nested loops, and side-effects in unstructured application code, you define an explicit graph where each node transforms a strongly-typed shared state.

flowchart LR
    START((START)) --> A[Setup]
    A --> B{Route}
    B -->|tools| C[Tool Execution]
    B -->|llm| D[LLM Generation]
    C --> B
    D --> END((END))

docs.title: Architecture & Core Primitives
docs.text: Component Type / Interface Responsibility State graph.State[T] Shared workflow memory. Must implement Copy() T. Builder *graph.Builder[S] Fluent API for registering nodes, edges, middleware, safety limits, and persistence. Node graph.Node[S] A unit of execution that accepts the current state and returns a Command. Node Function graph.NodeFunc[S] Adapter function to convert standard Go functions into a graph.Node[S]. Edge Direct, Conditional, Route Defines transitions between nodes. Command graph.Command[S] Instructions returned by nodes (Update, Interrupt, InterruptUpdate). Graph *graph.Graph[S] Immutable, compiled workflow engine created by builder.Build(). Snapshot graph.Snapshot[S] Point-in-time state snapshot including current values, next nodes, and location metadata.

docs.title: 1. State (graph.State[T])
docs.text:
Every Loom workflow operates on a user-defined Go struct that satisfies the generic graph.State[T] interface:

type State[T any] interface {
    Copy() T
}

docs.title: Writing a State Struct
docs.text:
Because Loom executes parallel nodes concurrently and supports checkpointing and time-travel, your Copy() method must ensure deep copy isolation for reference types (slices, maps, nested pointers):

package main

import "github.com/masterkeysrd/loom/message"

type AgentState struct {
    Query       string              `json:"query"`
    Messages    message.MessageList `json:"messages"`
    Iteration   int                 `json:"iteration"`
    NeedsReview bool                `json:"needs_review"`
    Output      string              `json:"output"`
}

// Copy creates an isolated copy of AgentState to prevent race conditions during execution.
func (s AgentState) Copy() AgentState {
    clone := s
    if s.Messages != nil {
        clone.Messages = make(message.MessageList, len(s.Messages))
        copy(clone.Messages, s.Messages)
    }
    return clone
}

[!TIP] Ensure all exported state fields include json tags. Loom checkpointers decompose state into channel-level JSON keys during persistence.

docs.title: 2. Commands: Directing the Engine
docs.text:
Nodes return a graph.Command[State] (and optional error) to notify the engine how state should change and whether execution should continue.

type Command[State any] interface {
    Apply(State) State
}

docs.title: Built-in Commands
docs.text:
• graph.Update[State](fn): Modifies state using a transformation function func(State) State. 

    return graph.Update[AgentState](func(s AgentState) AgentState {
    s.Iteration++
    return s
}), nil

  • graph.Interrupt(): Halts graph execution immediately. Loom persists the checkpoint to the configured checkpointer and returns the paused Snapshot to the caller. 

    if s.NeedsReview {
    return graph.Interrupt(), nil
}

  • graph.InterruptUpdate[State](fn): Modifies state and interrupts execution in a single atomic step. Used when a node (such as a sub-graph or a human-in-the-loop approval step) needs to record partial results before pausing. 

    return graph.InterruptUpdate[AgentState](func(s AgentState) AgentState {
    s.Output = "Waiting on user confirmation"
    return s
}), nil

docs.title: Defining Nodes with graph.NodeFunc
docs.text:
A node implements the graph.Node[State] interface:

type Node[State any] interface {
    Execute(context.Context, State) (Command[State], error)
}

Wrap inline functions cleanly with graph.NodeFunc[State]:

classifierNode := graph.NodeFunc[AgentState](func(ctx context.Context, state AgentState) (graph.Command[AgentState], error) {
    needsReview := len(state.Query) > 500
    return graph.Update[AgentState](func(s AgentState) AgentState {
        s.NeedsReview = needsReview
        return s
    }), nil
})

docs.title: Wiring Edges
docs.text:
Loom provides three types of edges to connect nodes:

  1. Unconditional Edges (AddEdge): Always transitions from source to destination. 

    builder.AddEdge(graph.START, "classify")
builder.AddEdge("execute", "summarize")
builder.AddEdge("summarize", graph.END)

  2. Conditional Edges (AddConditionalEdge): Branches based on a boolean predicate evaluated against current state. 

    builder.AddConditionalEdge("classify", "human_review", func(s AgentState) bool {
    return s.NeedsReview
})
builder.AddConditionalEdge("classify", "automated_process", func(s AgentState) bool {
    return !s.NeedsReview
})

  3. Route Edges (AddRouteEdge): Computes a route key dynamically and maps it to a target node. 

    builder.AddRouteEdge("decide", func(s AgentState) (string, error) {
    if s.Iteration > 3 {
        return "escalate", nil
    }
    return "retry", nil
}, map[string]string{
    "escalate": "manager_review",
    "retry":    "worker_node",
})

[!NOTE] graph.START and graph.END are reserved virtual nodes representing graph entry and termination points.

docs.title: 4. Parallel Node Execution (Fan-out / Fan-in)
docs.text:
Loom natively supports concurrent execution. When multiple outgoing edges emerge from a node (or from START), the engine executes target nodes in parallel using goroutines.

flowchart TD
    START((START)) --> A[Fetch Docs]
    START((START)) --> B[Fetch User Profile]
    START((START)) --> C[Fetch Permissions]
    A --> D[Synthesize Response]
    B --> D
    C --> D
    D --> END((END))

builder := graph.New[AgentState]()

// Fan-out: START branches into three parallel nodes
builder.AddEdge(graph.START, "fetchDocs")
builder.AddEdge(graph.START, "fetchUserProfile")
builder.AddEdge(graph.START, "fetchPermissions")

// Fan-in: all branches converge on a single aggregator node
builder.AddEdge("fetchDocs", "synthesize")
builder.AddEdge("fetchUserProfile", "synthesize")
builder.AddEdge("fetchPermissions", "synthesize")
builder.AddEdge("synthesize", graph.END)

docs.title: Parallel Execution Semantics
docs.text:
• State Isolation: Before invoking each branch, Loom clones the current snapshot via snapshot.State.Copy(). Parallel nodes execute concurrently without shared memory race conditions.
  • Deterministic Merge: Commands returned by parallel nodes are collected and applied sequentially in slice/edge order: 
    applyAll := func(s State) State {
    for _, cmd := range cmds {
        if cmd != nil {
            s = cmd.Apply(s)
        }
    }
    return s
}
  • Fan-in Deduplication: When multiple parallel edges converge on the same target (such as "synthesize" above), Loom deduplicates the downstream node list while preserving encounter order. The join node runs exactly once.
  • Error Handling: If any concurrent node returns an error, execution stops immediately, and Loom returns the first encountered error formatted as failed to execute node: %w.
  • Interrupt Handling: If any concurrent node returns an Interruptable command (like Interrupt() or InterruptUpdate), the merged result is promoted to an interrupt, pausing execution and saving the updated state.
  • Safety Step Tracking: Every executed parallel node increments the execution step counter against the configured WithMaxSteps limit.

docs.title: 5. Sub-graphs as Nodes (AsNode & MapNode)
docs.text: Sub-graphs enable composable, hierarchical agent architectures. A sub-graph is an independently defined, fully compiled Graph embedded as a node inside a parent graph.

docs.title: Same-State Sub-graphs (childGraph.AsNode())
docs.text:
When child and parent share the exact same state struct, convert the compiled child graph directly with .AsNode():

// 1. Build the child research graph
childBuilder := graph.New[AgentState]().WithName("researcher")
childBuilder.AddNode("search", searchNode)
childBuilder.AddNode("summarize", summarizeNode)
childBuilder.AddEdge(graph.START, "search")
childBuilder.AddEdge("search", "summarize")
childBuilder.AddEdge("summarize", graph.END)
childGraph, _ := childBuilder.Build()

// 2. Embed inside parent coordinator graph
parentBuilder := graph.New[AgentState]().WithName("coordinator")
parentBuilder.AddNode("setup", setupNode)
parentBuilder.AddNode("research", childGraph.AsNode()) // <-- Sub-graph node
parentBuilder.AddNode("deliver", deliverNode)

parentBuilder.AddEdge(graph.START, "setup")
parentBuilder.AddEdge("setup", "research")
parentBuilder.AddEdge("research", "deliver")
parentBuilder.AddEdge("deliver", graph.END)

parentGraph, _ := parentBuilder.Build()

docs.title: Different-State Sub-graphs (graph.MapNode)
docs.text:
When a sub-graph requires a specialized child state, use graph.MapNode to adapt parent state to child state and back:

type ParentState struct {
    UserID      string `json:"user_id"`
    RawQuestion string `json:"raw_question"`
    Answer      string `json:"answer"`
}

func (s ParentState) Copy() ParentState { return s }

type MathState struct {
    Expression string  `json:"expression"`
    Result     float64 `json:"result"`
}

func (s MathState) Copy() MathState { return s }

// childMathGraph operates on MathState
mathGraph, _ := mathBuilder.Build()

// Adapt mathGraph to parent's ParentState
mathNode := graph.MapNode(
    mathGraph.AsNode(),
    // toChild: extract ChildState from ParentState
    func(parent ParentState) MathState {
        return MathState{Expression: parent.RawQuestion}
    },
    // fromChild: integrate ChildState updates back into ParentState
    func(parent ParentState, child MathState) ParentState {
        parent.Answer = fmt.Sprintf("Result: %.2f", child.Result)
        return parent
    },
)

parentBuilder.AddNode("calculator", mathNode)

docs.title: Hierarchical Checkpoint Namespaces
docs.text:
When saving checkpoints across nested sub-graphs, Loom scopes state storage into LangGraph-style hierarchical namespaces:

$$\text{CheckpointNS} = \langle\text{parent_ns}\rangle \mid \langle\text{node_name}\rangle:\langle\text{task_id}\rangle$$

Examples: - Root level: "" (empty string) - First sub-graph level: "research:83a1b0fe..." - Nested sub-graph level: "research:83a1b0fe...|web_search:c593d18e..."

docs.title: Namespace Guarantees:
docs.text:
1. Deterministic Task IDs: Loom derives task_id deterministically via SHA-1 of (ThreadID, CheckpointNS, Step, NodeName).
  2. Interrupt & Resume Isolation: When a sub-graph interrupts, the parent location preserves the execution step counter. On resume, the sub-graph receives the exact same CheckpointNS and picks up directly from its last saved child checkpoint.
  3. Loop Separation: Loops across distinct graph steps compute different task IDs, preventing collisions across repeated iterations.
  4. Node Name Restrictions: Because | is the namespace separator (NSSep) and : is the task separator (NSEnd), node names cannot contain | or :. Slashes (e.g. "tools/search" or "agent/writer") are fully supported.

docs.title: Interrupt Propagation
docs.text: If any node inside a sub-graph returns an Interrupt() or InterruptUpdate: 1. Sub-graph execution halts and persists its internal child checkpoint. 2. AsNode() or MapNode catches the incomplete snapshot (!snap.IsDone()). 3. AsNode() / MapNode returns an InterruptUpdate command to the parent engine. 4. The parent graph pauses, records all mutations up to the interrupt point, and returns the snapshot to the caller.

docs.title: 6. Execution Safety (WithMaxSteps)
docs.text:
Cyclic agent workflows (e.g. reflection loops, tool-retry cycles) can risk infinite execution if an exit condition is never reached. Loom provides rigorous safeguards:

builder := graph.New[AgentState]().
    WithMaxSteps(25) // Limit total node executions to 25

g, _ := builder.Build()

snapshot, err := g.Execute(ctx, initialCmd, nil)
if errors.Is(err, graph.ErrMaxStepsExceeded) {
    log.Printf("Safety limit reached: %v", err)
}
  • Step Counting: Virtual START is not counted. Each invoked user node (including parallel nodes) increments the step count.
  • Dynamic Override: You can also set or adjust limits after building via g.SetMaxSteps(limit).
  • Context Cancellation: Loom validates ctx.Err() at every loop iteration and aborts immediately if a context deadline or cancellation occurs.

docs.title: 7. Node Middleware & Retry Policies
docs.text:
Loom middleware allows you to intercept, wrap, log, and retry user node executions without polluting node business logic.

type Middleware[S any] func(Node[S]) Node[S]

Middlewares are applied in registered order (outermost first) and wrap only real user nodes (virtual START and END are never wrapped).

func LoggingMiddleware[S any](logger *log.Logger) graph.Middleware[S] {
    return func(next graph.Node[S]) graph.Node[S] {
        return graph.NodeFunc[S](func(ctx context.Context, state S) (graph.Command[S], error) {
            logger.Printf("entering node execution")
            cmd, err := next.Execute(ctx, state)
            logger.Printf("exiting node execution with err=%v", err)
            return cmd, err
        })
    }
}

builder.WithMiddleware(LoggingMiddleware[AgentState](logger))

docs.title: Configurable Retry Middleware (RetryMiddleware)
docs.text:
Loom provides a built-in exponential backoff RetryMiddleware for transient failures (e.g. network timeouts, LLM rate limits):

retryPolicy := graph.RetryMiddleware[AgentState](
    graph.WithMaxAttempts(4),                    // Total attempts including initial call (default: 3)
    graph.WithInitialWait(200*time.Millisecond), // Initial wait duration (default: 100ms)
    graph.WithMaxWait(10*time.Second),           // Max wait cap (default: 5s)
    graph.WithMultiplier(2.0),                   // Exponential multiplier (default: 2.0)
    graph.WithShouldRetry(func(err error) bool { // Optional retry predicate
        // Skip retrying non-transient validation errors
        return !errors.Is(err, ErrBadRequest)
    }),
)

builder.WithMiddleware(retryPolicy)

docs.title: Retry Middleware Safety:
docs.text:
• State Isolation: Before each retry attempt, RetryMiddleware clones state with state.Copy(), guaranteeing failed runs do not contaminate retry attempts.
  • Cancellation Awareness: If ctx.Done() triggers during backoff wait or node execution, the middleware stops immediately and returns ctx.Err().

docs.title: 8. Visualization (ToMermaid & MermaidURL)
docs.text:
Compile and visualize your graph structure for documentation, debugging, or Loom Studio rendering:

g, _ := builder.Build()

// Generate raw Mermaid diagram definition
mermaidText := g.ToMermaid()
fmt.Println(mermaidText)

// Generate instant preview link via mermaid.ink
imageURL := g.MermaidURL()
fmt.Println("Graph Diagram Preview:", imageURL)

Example Mermaid output: 

graph TD
  START((START))
  classify[classify]
  human_review[human_review]
  automated_process[automated_process]
  END((END))
  START --> classify
  classify -. [conditional] .-> human_review
  classify -. [conditional] .-> automated_process
  human_review --> END
  automated_process --> END

docs.title: 8. Compile-Time Graph Validation
docs.text:
Loom strictly validates graph topology and integrity when builder.Build() is called, catching structural configuration mistakes before execution begins:

g, err := builder.Build()
if err != nil {
    log.Fatalf("invalid graph configuration: %v", err)
}

docs.title: Validation Guarantees:
docs.text:
• Node Validation: Node names cannot be empty, reserved (START, END), or contain namespace delimiters (|, :). Nodes cannot be nil.
  • Entry & Terminal Integrity: The graph must declare at least one outgoing edge from START. The terminal END node cannot have outgoing edges.
  • Dead-End Detection: Every user-defined node must define at least one outgoing edge (to another node or to END).
  • Edge & Target Integrity: All edges must originate from known nodes and point to valid, registered destination nodes (edges cannot point back to START).
  • Edge Predicate Integrity: Conditions for ConditionalEdge and routing functions/target maps for RouteEdge cannot be empty or nil.

docs.title: Next Steps
docs.text:
• Persistence & State: Explore SQLite, PostgreSQL, and checkpoint storage.
  • Human-in-the-Loop: Build interactive approval and review loops.
  • Tools & Streaming: Stream LLM output and connect external agent tools.
  • RAG Workflows: Ingest documents, create vector stores, and retrieve knowledge.

docs.title: Human-in-the-Loop (HITL) 🤝
docs.text: Human-in-the-loop patterns allow you to pause an AI workflow and wait for human approval, clarification, or additional input. This is critical for high-stakes tasks where an LLM should not act autonomously (e.g., executing financial transactions, sending external emails, or approving destructive operations).

docs.title: 1. The Interrupt Pattern
docs.text: Loom provides two first-class commands to pause execution and record checkpoints:

docs.title: Basic Interrupt: graph.Interrupt()
docs.text:
Use graph.Interrupt() to halt execution immediately without modifying the state. Loom persists the current state to the configured checkpointer and returns the paused Snapshot to the caller.

builder.AddNode("Review", graph.NodeFunc[MyState](func(ctx context.Context, s MyState) (graph.Command[MyState], error) {
    if s.RequiresApproval && !s.IsApproved {
        // Stop execution and save checkpoint
        return graph.Interrupt(), nil 
    }
    return graph.Update[MyState](func(s MyState) MyState { return s }), nil
}))

docs.title: Interrupt with State Update: graph.InterruptUpdate[S]
docs.text:
Often an agent must mutate the state before pausing—for example, recording the question being asked to the human, updating a status flag to "awaiting_approval", or caching draft responses:

builder.AddNode("PrepareApproval", graph.NodeFunc[MyState](func(ctx context.Context, s MyState) (graph.Command[MyState], error) {
    // Modify state AND pause execution in a single atomic operation
    return graph.InterruptUpdate[MyState](func(state MyState) MyState {
        state.Status = "awaiting_human_approval"
        state.ReviewPrompt = "Please confirm the transfer of $5,000 to Account #1234."
        state.PendingActionID = "tx-994"
        return state
    }), nil
}))

graph.InterruptUpdate[S] implements graph.Interruptable. When the engine detects this command, it applies the state transformation, marks the snapshot as interrupted (!snapshot.IsDone()), and persists the updated state into the checkpoint before returning.

docs.title: 2. Waiting for Input & Resuming
docs.text:
When a graph interrupts, Graph.Execute returns a Snapshot whose IsDone() method returns false. You can present the current state to a user (e.g., via a web UI, Slack bot, or CLI) and wait for feedback:

// 1. Initial execution runs until PrepareApproval interrupts
snapshot, err := g.Execute(ctx, initialInput, &graph.Location{ThreadID: "order-994"})
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}

if !snapshot.IsDone() {
    fmt.Printf("Workflow paused at step %d. Prompt: %s\n", snapshot.Location.CheckpointID, snapshot.State.ReviewPrompt)
}

// ... User clicks "Approve" in the dashboard ...

// 2. Resume execution by providing the human's input and passing the saved Location
humanInput := graph.Update[MyState](func(s MyState) MyState {
    s.IsApproved = true
    s.Status = "approved"
    return s
})

// Resume from the previous checkpoint location
resumedSnapshot, err := g.Execute(ctx, humanInput, &snapshot.Location)

docs.title: 3. Subgraph Interrupt Propagation (AsNode & MapNode)
docs.text:
When building modular, hierarchical agents with sub-graphs (childGraph.AsNode() or graph.MapNode), interrupt handling is fully transparent:

flowchart TD
    subgraph Parent Graph
        A[Start] --> B[Sub-graph Node]
        B --> C[Finalize]
    end
    subgraph Child Sub-graph
        B1[Child Step 1] --> B2[Human Review Node]
        B2 -->|Interrupt| B2_PAUSE[Child Pause & Checkpoint]
    end
    B2_PAUSE -.->|InterruptUpdate| B

docs.title: How Subgraph Interrupts Work:
docs.text:
1. Child Interruption: When a node inside the sub-graph returns graph.Interrupt() or graph.InterruptUpdate[ChildState], the child graph pauses and saves its internal checkpoint under its scoped namespace (e.g., coordinator|reviewer:sha1...).
  2. Parent Propagation: AsNode() and MapNode detect that the sub-graph run did not complete (!childSnapshot.IsDone()). They wrap the child's partial state in a parent InterruptUpdate command.
  3. Parent Checkpointing: The parent graph updates its state and pauses, creating a parent checkpoint.
  4. Seamless Resumption: When you resume the parent graph via g.Execute(ctx, input, &parentSnapshot.Location), the sub-graph is re-entered with the exact same namespace and step index, resuming the child graph directly from its paused state without restarting from the beginning.

docs.title: 4. State Forking (Time Travel)
docs.text:
Because Loom uses checkpoints, you can "go back in time" by resuming from an older checkpoint with different inputs. This is useful for testing different decision paths or correcting an agent's mistakes.

// Resume from a specific historical checkpoint ID
forkLocation := &graph.Location{
    ThreadID:     "order-994",
    CheckpointID: "0194689b-8c81-7925-950e-b7d5eb85bf22", // Prior checkpoint ID
}

snapshot, err := g.Execute(ctx, correctionCommand, forkLocation)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• graph.Interrupt(): Pause execution and save current state without mutations.
  • graph.InterruptUpdate[S]: Atomically mutate state and trigger an interrupt.
  • Subgraph Propagation: AsNode() and MapNode automatically bubble interrupts to the parent workflow while maintaining checkpoint namespaces.
  • Resumption: Provide new input and resume from a saved Location.
  • Time Travel: Fork from any historical CheckpointID to explore alternate execution branches.

docs.title: LLM Package 🧠
docs.text: The llm package provides a high-level abstraction over different Large Language Model (LLM) backends. It allows you to interact with models from various providers (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Ollama) using a consistent API.

docs.title: Core Components
docs.text:
• Model: The primary interface for interacting with an LLM. It supports both blocking (Invoke) and streaming (Stream) calls.
  • Provider: The backend-specific implementation that translates generic requests into provider-specific API calls.
  • Registry: A central store for managing and instantiating providers without creating hard dependencies.

docs.title: 1. Using the Model API
docs.text:
The llm.Model provides a fluent API for configuring and calling LLMs.

import (
    "github.com/masterkeysrd/loom/llm"
    "github.com/masterkeysrd/loom/providers/openai"
)

// 1. Create a provider
provider, _ := loomopenai.NewDefaultProvider()

// 2. Instantiate a model
model := llm.NewModel(provider, "gpt-4o")

// 3. Configure parameters (Fluent API)
model = model.
    WithTemperature(0.7).
    WithMaxTokens(1000).
    WithStop("User:", "Assistant:")

// 4. Invoke the model (blocking)
resp, err := model.Invoke(ctx, messages)

// 5. Stream the model (real-time)
// Chunks are automatically forwarded to any stream.Writer in the context.
stream, err := model.Stream(ctx, messages)
for chunk, err := range stream {
    fmt.Print(chunk.Content.Text())
}

docs.title: Structured Output (JSON Schema)
docs.text:
If a provider supports it, you can enforce a specific JSON schema for the model's response. 

model = model.WithStructuredOutput(myJsonSchema)

docs.title: Thinking (Reasoning) Mode
docs.text:
For models that support "thinking" or extended reasoning (like Anthropic Claude or Google Gemini), you can configure the reasoning budget. 

model = model.WithThinking(4000) // 4000 tokens for thinking

docs.title: Extensions & Hints
docs.text:
Providers often have specialized features (like caching) that aren't part of the common LLM parameters. Loom uses a type-safe Extensions system to pass these hints.

Extensions come in two flavors: 1. Call Extensions (llm.Extension): Apply to the entire request (e.g., enable system prompt caching). 2. Message Extensions (message.Extension): Apply to a specific turn in the conversation (e.g., mark a checkpoint).

// Example: Setting a call-level extension for Anthropic
model = model.WithExtension(loomanthropic.PromptCaching{CacheHeader: true})

// Example: Passing a call-level extension for a single call
model.Invoke(ctx, msgs, llm.WithExtensionOption(loomopenai.PromptCache{
    Key: "user-session-123",
}))

docs.title: 3. Middleware & Hooks
docs.text:
Middleware allows you to wrap LLM calls to inject cross-cutting concerns like logging, auditing, or automatic metadata injection.

model = model.WithMiddleware(func(next llm.Streamer) llm.Streamer {
    return func(ctx context.Context, req *llm.Request) (llm.StreamResponse, error) {
        fmt.Printf("Calling model: %s\n", req.Model)

        // You can also modify the request before it reaches the provider
        if len(req.Messages) > 10 {
            req.Extensions[myprovider.CustomExt{}.ExtensionID()] = myprovider.CustomExt{Enabled: true}
        }

        return next(ctx, req)
    }
})

docs.title: 4. Cache Management
docs.text:
For providers that support explicit resource management (like Google Gemini's Context Caching), Loom provides a CacheManager API.

// 1. Create a long-lived cache from a list of messages
cacheID, err := model.
    WithExtension(loomgenai.CacheCreation{DisplayName: "Project Docs"}).
    CreateCache(ctx, documentMessages)

// 2. Use the cache ID in subsequent calls
resp, _ := model.Invoke(ctx, prompt, llm.WithExtensionOption(loomgenai.ContextCache{ID: cacheID}))

// 3. Delete when no longer needed
model.DeleteCache(ctx, cacheID)

docs.title: 5. Quota & Rate Limit Inspection (llm.QuotaProvider)
docs.text:
Providers that expose quota or rolling-window capacity metrics (such as Google Antigravity) implement the llm.QuotaProvider interface. This allows callers to inspect remaining capacity percentages and reset times:

// Type-assert to llm.QuotaProvider
if qp, ok := provider.(llm.QuotaProvider); ok {
    // Inspect a specific model (resolves aliases like "gemini-3.8-flash")
    if quota, ok, err := qp.GetQuota(ctx, "gemini-3.8-flash"); ok && err == nil {
        fmt.Printf("Remaining: %.1f%%\n", quota.Percentage())
        if reset, err := quota.ParsedResetTime(); err == nil && !reset.IsZero() {
            fmt.Printf("Replenishes at: %s\n", reset.Format(time.RFC3339))
        }
    }

    // List all model quotas
    quotas, _ := qp.ListQuotas(ctx)
    for model, q := range quotas {
        fmt.Printf("• %s: %.1f%%\n", model, q.Percentage())
    }
}

docs.title: 6. Using the LLM Registry
docs.text: The Registry is useful for decoupling your application from specific provider packages. It allows you to register provider factories and retrieve them by name.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• Use llm.NewModel to start interacting with an LLM.
  • Use the With* methods to configure model parameters.
  • Use Invoke for simple request-response and Stream for real-time applications.
  • Use llm.QuotaProvider to query model quotas and replenishment windows.
  • Use llm.Registry to manage multiple providers in a large application.

docs.title: Model Context Protocol (MCP) 🔌
docs.text:
The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is an open standard that enables developers to build secure, two-way connections between AI applications and external data sources, tools, and prompts.

Loom provides first-class support for MCP, implementing MCP v2 (2026-07-28) with automatic fallback to legacy MCP v1 (2025-11-25). Loom manages connection pooling, transport negotiation, authentication, and multi-server orchestration through a clean, unified Go API.

docs.title: 1. Core Abstractions
docs.text:
Loom's MCP implementation centers around the following types:

  • Client: A pooled client for an individual MCP server. It manages session pooling, idle timeouts (5-minute default), and automatic reconnection transparently.
  • MultiClient: A registry managing multiple named MCP servers simultaneously (mc.Tools(ctx, "serverName"), mc.GetPrompt(...)).
  • Config: Defines connection parameters, transport (stdio or http), protocol version negotiation, timeouts, authentication, and elicitation.
  • AuthProvider: Dynamic authentication handlers for OAuth2 Authorization Code, Client Credentials (M2M), and Enterprise OIDC flows.
  • ElicitationProvider: Interactive handlers for server-initiated user input requests (Form and URL modes).

docs.title: 2. MCP v2 (2026-07-28) Capabilities
docs.text: Loom includes native support for the MCP v2 specification (ProtocolVersion20260728):

docs.title: Stateless server/discover Negotiation
docs.text: When establishing a connection, Loom negotiates protocol version 2026-07-28 via stateless discovery (server/discover). If the server only supports MCP v1, Loom automatically falls back to the legacy stateful initialize handshake (ProtocolVersion20251125).

docs.title: Stateless Subscriptions (subscriptions/listen, SEP-2575)
docs.text: Under MCP v2, persistent standalone SSE GET streams are replaced by request-scoped streamable HTTP transports and stateless subscription listening via subscriptions/listen.

docs.title: Client-Side TTL Caching (SEP-2549)
docs.text: Loom's MCP transport honors server-provided cache controls and expiration metadata, enabling low-latency responses for static resource listings and tool definitions.

docs.title: Multi Round-Trip Request Handling (SEP-2322)
docs.text: During complex tool execution, MCP servers can issue intermediate InputRequest payloads (such as requesting missing arguments, OAuth scopes, or interactive confirmations). Loom automatically captures these elicitation requests, passes them to your ElicitationProvider, and retries the call with InputResponse and preserved RequestState.

docs.title: Safety Annotations & Tool Adaptation
docs.text:
Tools returned by an MCP server are automatically adapted to Loom's native tool.Tool format: - OutputSchema: Fully preserved and mapped for structured output validation. - Safety Annotation: Captures behavioral hints: - IsReadOnly: Inferred from ReadOnlyHint. - IsIdempotent: Inferred from IdempotentHint. - IsDangerous: Inferred from DestructiveHint or !ReadOnlyHint. - IsOpenWorld: Inferred from OpenWorldHint (defaults to true). - ResourceLink: Rich MCP resource links are converted to message.TextBlock with metadata extras (type: "resource_link", uri, title, name, description, mime_type).

[!NOTE] MCP Logging Deprecation (SEP-2577): In protocol version 2026-07-28, protocol-level logging notifications (OnLogMessage, SetLoggingLevel) are deprecated in favor of standard OpenTelemetry tracing/metrics and process stderr.

docs.title: 3. Configuration (mcp.Config)
docs.text:
Each server is configured via an mcp.Config struct:

// 1. Local subprocess (stdio)
stdioConfig := mcp.Config{
    Transport: "stdio",
    Command:   "python",
    Args:      []string{"my_mcp_server.py"},
    Env:       map[string]string{"DEBUG": "true"},
}

// 2. Remote Streamable HTTP (MCP v2)
httpConfig := mcp.Config{
    Transport:            "http",
    URL:                  "https://mcp.internal.example.com",
    Headers:              map[string]string{"X-Api-Key": "secret-key"},
    ProtocolVersion:      mcp.ProtocolVersion20260728, // Optional: defaults to latest
    DisableStandaloneSSE: true,                       // Recommended for v2
    MaxRetries:           3,
}

docs.title: Config Options Reference
docs.text: Field Type Description Transport string "stdio" or "http". Command / Args / Env string, []string, map Command executable, arguments, and environment variables for stdio. URL string Endpoint URL for remote HTTP servers. Headers map[string]string Static headers (e.g., API keys, static Bearer tokens). ProtocolVersion string Optional version override (ProtocolVersion20260728 or ProtocolVersion20251125). Defaults to negotiating 2026-07-28. DisableStandaloneSSE bool Disables standalone GET SSE streams on HTTP connections (recommended for MCP v2). MaxRetries int Maximum reconnection attempts for HTTP streams. DisableMultiRoundTrip bool Disables automatic SEP-2322 Multi Round-Trip request elicitation handling. Auth AuthProvider Dynamic authentication provider (OAuth2, Client Credentials, Enterprise). Elicitation ElicitationProvider Handler for interactive user input (Form and URL modes).

docs.title: 4. Integrating Tools with Loom
docs.text:
Loom's Client maintains a pooled session with an idle timer. You call client.Tools(ctx) directly on the client without manual session setup:

package main

import (
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "log"

    "github.com/masterkeysrd/loom/mcp"
    "github.com/masterkeysrd/loom/tool"
)

func main() {
    ctx := context.Background()

    // 1. Configure and instantiate client
    client := mcp.NewClient(mcp.Config{
        Transport: "stdio",
        Command:   "npx",
        Args:      []string{"-y", "@modelcontextprotocol/server-everything"},
    })
    defer client.Close()

    // 2. Fetch tools (adapted to native Loom tools)
    tools, err := client.Tools(ctx)
    if err != nil {
        log.Fatalf("Failed to fetch tools: %v", err)
    }

    for _, t := range tools {
        fmt.Printf("Tool: %-20s ReadOnly: %-5v Dangerous: %-5v\n", 
            t.Definition.Name, 
            t.Definition.Annotation.IsReadOnly, 
            t.Definition.Annotation.IsDangerous,
        )
    }

    // 3. Register with Loom tool container
    container := tool.NewContainer(tools...)

    // 4. Bind container definitions to an LLM model
    // model = model.BindToolDefs(container.Definitions()...)
}

docs.title: Calling Tools Directly
docs.text:
You can also execute tools directly via client.CallTool:

stream, err := client.CallTool(ctx, "echo", map[string]any{"message": "Hello MCP!"})
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}

for chunk, err := range stream {
    if err != nil {
        log.Fatal(err)
    }
    // Access streamed text content
    if chunk.Content != nil {
        fmt.Print(chunk.Content.Text())
    }
    // Access structured JSON output (if provided by server)
    if chunk.StructuredContent != nil {
        fmt.Printf("Structured: %+v\n", chunk.StructuredContent)
    }
}

docs.title: 5. Resources and Prompts
docs.text: In addition to tools, MCP servers can expose structured data resources and prompt templates.

docs.title: Resources
docs.text:
Query resources directly using the pooled client:

// 1. List available resources
resources, err := client.Resources(ctx)
for _, r := range resources {
    fmt.Printf("Resource: %s (%s, %d bytes)\n", r.URI, r.MIMEType, r.Size)
}

// 2. Read specific resources (returns Loom message.Content blocks)
content, err := client.GetResources(ctx, []string{"file:///logs/app.log"})
for _, block := range content {
    fmt.Println("Resource text:", block.Text())
}

// 3. Subscribe to real-time resource updates
err = client.SubscribeResource(ctx, "file:///logs/app.log")

docs.title: Prompt Templates
docs.text:
Retrieve prompt templates ready for injection into conversation histories:

// 1. List available prompts
prompts, err := client.Prompts(ctx)
for _, p := range prompts {
    fmt.Printf("Prompt: %s - %s\n", p.Name, p.Description)
}

// 2. Fetch prompt with argument substitution (returns []message.Message)
messages, err := client.GetPrompt(ctx, "code_review", map[string]string{
    "language": "Go",
    "diff":     gitDiffOutput,
})

// 3. Append to conversation history
conversation = append(conversation, messages...)

docs.title: 6. Multi-Server Management (MultiClient)
docs.text:
When your application integrates multiple MCP servers (e.g., GitHub, Postgres, Slack), manage them through a MultiClient:

configs := map[string]mcp.Config{
    "postgres": {
        Transport: "stdio",
        Command:   "mcp-server-postgres",
        Args:      []string{"--conn", "postgres://localhost/mydb"},
    },
    "weather": {
        Transport: "http",
        URL:       "https://weather.mcp.example.com",
    },
}

mc := mcp.NewMultiClient(configs)
defer mc.Close()

// Query tools from the postgres server
dbTools, err := mc.Tools(ctx, "postgres")

// Query prompts from the weather server
prompts, err := mc.Prompts(ctx, "weather")

// Check individual server health
status, err := mc.Status("postgres")
fmt.Println("Postgres server status:", status)

// Restart an individual server connection if needed
err = mc.Restart(ctx, "postgres")

docs.title: 7. Authentication (mcp/auth.go)
docs.text: Loom provides built-in authentication handlers for securing remote MCP connections:

docs.title: Static Authentication
docs.text:
For simple bearer tokens or static API keys, supply headers in mcp.Config:

config := mcp.Config{
    Transport: "http",
    URL:       "https://api.example.com/mcp",
    Headers: map[string]string{
        "Authorization": "Bearer my-static-api-token",
    },
}

docs.title: Interactive OAuth2 (mcp.OAuth2Provider)
docs.text:
For user-facing CLI or desktop tools requiring the standard OAuth2 Authorization Code flow:

config := mcp.Config{
    Transport: "http",
    URL:       "https://mcp.service.com",
    Auth: &mcp.OAuth2Provider{
        ClientID:     "my-client-id",
        ClientSecret: "my-client-secret", // Optional for public PKCE clients
        RedirectPort: 3142,               // Local callback port (defaults to 3142)
    },
}
When connecting, Loom spins up a local loopback server on the redirect port and prompts the user to complete authorization in their browser.

docs.title: Headless M2M OAuth2 (mcp.ClientCredentialsProvider)
docs.text:
For backend services, cron jobs, and daemons requiring machine-to-machine authentication without user intervention:

config := mcp.Config{
    Transport: "http",
    URL:       "https://mcp.service.com",
    Auth: &mcp.ClientCredentialsProvider{
        ClientID:     os.Getenv("MCP_CLIENT_ID"),
        ClientSecret: os.Getenv("MCP_CLIENT_SECRET"),
    },
}

docs.title: Enterprise Managed Authorization (mcp.EnterpriseProvider)
docs.text:
For enterprise deployments requiring Single Sign-On (OIDC) through an identity provider (e.g., Okta, Entra ID) and downstream token exchange with an MCP authorization server:

config := mcp.Config{
    Transport: "http",
    URL:       "https://enterprise-mcp.internal",
    Auth: &mcp.EnterpriseProvider{
        ClientID:         "my-oidc-client-id",
        ClientSecret:     os.Getenv("OIDC_CLIENT_SECRET"),
        RedirectPort:     3142,
        IdPIssuerURL:     "https://login.okta.com/oauth2/default",
        MCPAuthServerURL: "https://auth.internal.corp",
        MCPResourceURI:   "urn:mcp:enterprise:data",
    },
}

docs.title: 8. Multi Round-Trip Elicitation (SEP-2322)
docs.text:
When an MCP server requires interactive input or user confirmation during tool execution, Loom delegates the request to your ElicitationProvider:

type InteractiveElicitationHandler struct{}

func (h *InteractiveElicitationHandler) HandleElicit(ctx context.Context, params *mcp.ElicitParams) (*mcp.ElicitResult, error) {
    // Inspect elicitation mode (Form or URL)
    fmt.Printf("Server requested input: %s\n", params.Message)

    // Form elicitation: collect user inputs
    // URL elicitation: prompt user to complete an external browser action
    return &mcp.ElicitResult{
        Action: "accept",
        Content: map[string]any{
            "confirmation": true,
        },
    }, nil
}

func (h *InteractiveElicitationHandler) HandleElicitComplete(ctx context.Context, params *mcp.ElicitationCompleteParams) {
    fmt.Println("Elicitation complete for ID:", params.ElicitationID)
}

// Attach to Config
config := mcp.Config{
    Transport:   "http",
    URL:         "https://mcp.service.com",
    Elicitation: &InteractiveElicitationHandler{},
}

Loom automatically submits the InputResponse back to the server and resumes tool execution without breaking agent workflows.

docs.title: 9. Observability & OpenTelemetry
docs.text:
All MCP tool invocations through client.CallTool are automatically instrumented with OpenTelemetry:

  • Client Spans: Named tools/call with standard semantic attributes:
  • rpc.system.name = "jsonrpc"
  • rpc.method = "tools/call"
  • gen_ai.tool.name = "<toolName>"
  • loom.tool.type = "mcp"
  • Trace Context Propagation: Active trace and span context is injected into the MCP JSON-RPC call metadata (params.Meta), enabling distributed tracing across microservices and subprocesses.
  • Latency & Error Recording: Duration and status codes are reported via OpenTelemetry metrics.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• Use mcp.NewClient with mcp.Config to connect to stdio or HTTP servers.
  • Use client.Tools(ctx) directly on the pooled client—no manual session management required.
  • Take advantage of MCP v2 (2026-07-28) stateless discovery, subscriptions, caching, and multi-round-trip elicitation.
  • Authenticate with OAuth2Provider, ClientCredentialsProvider, or EnterpriseProvider.
  • Manage fleets of MCP servers with mcp.NewMultiClient.

docs.title: Memory & Context Management 🧠
docs.text: As conversations with AI agents grow, they can quickly exceed the LLM's context window (token limit). Loom provides automated tools to manage this history through Trimming and Summarization.

docs.title: 1. Trimming Messages
docs.text:
Trimming is a simple way to keep only the most recent messages. Loom provides a flexible Trimmer that can handle different strategies.

trimmed, _ := message.TrimMessages(ctx, history, 4000, &message.TrimConfig{
    Strategy:      message.TrimStrategyLast, // Keep the N most recent tokens
    IncludeSystem: true,                     // Always keep the system instruction
})

docs.title: Trimming Strategies
docs.text:
• TrimStrategyLast: Keeps the most recent messages that fit within the token limit.
  • TrimStrategyFirst: Keeps the oldest messages (rarely used for history).

docs.title: 2. Automatic Summarization
docs.text: Summarization is a more advanced technique where the agent "remembers" the gist of the conversation by condensing old messages into a summary.

docs.title: Setting up a Summarizer
docs.text:
import "github.com/masterkeysrd/loom/memory"

summarizer, _ := memory.NewSummarizer(model, memory.SummarizerConfig{
    TokenCounter: modelProvider.(llm.TokenCounter),
    Triggers: []memory.SummarizerTrigger{
        // Summarize when the conversation exceeds 4000 tokens
        memory.TriggerSummaryOnTokenCount(4000),
    },
})

docs.title: Using the Summarizer in a Node
docs.text:
func llmNode(ctx context.Context, s MyState) (graph.Command[AppState], error) {
    // 1. Summarize if a trigger is met
    newHistory, _ := summarizer.Summarize(ctx, s.Messages)

    // 2. Invoke the model with the condensed history
    resp, _ := model.Invoke(ctx, newHistory)

    return graph.Update(func(s MyState) MyState {
        s.Messages = append(newHistory, resp)
        return s
    }), nil
}

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
• Combine Strategies: Use summarization for long-term "memory" and trimming as a safety net to ensure you never exceed hard limits.
  • System Message: Always preserve your system instruction (prompt) during trimming/summarization.
  • Token Accuracy: Use the TokenCounter provided by your LLM provider for the most accurate results.

docs.title: Observability
docs.text: Loom provides first-class support for observability using OpenTelemetry (OTel). This allows you to trace the execution of your agents, monitor performance, and debug complex multi-step workflows.

docs.title: Quick Start
docs.text:
The easiest way to get started is to use the built-in telemetry package and Loom Studio.

import "github.com/masterkeysrd/loom/telemetry"

// Initialize telemetry (usually in main)
shutdown, _ := telemetry.Init(ctx, telemetry.Config{ServiceName: "my-agent"})
defer shutdown(ctx)

// Start a span
ctx, span := telemetry.Start(ctx, "my-operation")
defer span.End()

// Log a custom attribute
span.SetAttributes(telemetry.WithLoomThread("thread-123"))

docs.title: Loom Studio
